definition:
The fear of the LORD is the reverent awe of a creature before the living God, an awe that takes in both his majesty and his mercy and so shapes everything a person does. It is not terror that drives a person away from God, and it is not mere politeness toward him. It is the settled recognition that God is God, holy, great, near, and able to judge, joined with trust that this God is good. In Scripture it shows itself in worship, in obedience, in turning from evil, in honest dealing when no human court is watching, and in freedom from the fear of other people. Proverbs calls it the beginning of knowledge and wisdom; Deuteronomy sets it beside love as what God asks of his people. The study of holiness treats who God is in his purity and majesty; this study follows the human response to him that Scripture calls fear.

The main Hebrew word is the verb yare', ‘to fear’, with the adjective yare', ‘fearing’ (often a noun, ‘one who fears’), and the noun yir'ah, ‘fear’. Together they occur hundreds of times, and their range runs from plain fright (Genesis 3:10) to reverence and worship. Context decides the sense, which is why the Berean Standard Bible can translate the same Hebrew as ‘worship’ in Jonah 1:9 (literally ‘the LORD, the God of the heavens, I fear’) and 2 Kings 17:33. Other words sharpen the picture: pachad, ‘dread’, which gives God the title “the Fear of Isaac” (Genesis 31:42) and stands in Psalm 36:1; and mora', ‘object of fear’ (Isaiah 8:13). In Greek the Septuagint and the New Testament use phobos, ‘fear’, and the verb phobeomai, which carry the same range from panic to reverence, along with eulabeia, ‘reverence’ or ‘godly fear’ (Hebrews 5:7; 12:28), and deos, ‘awe’ (Hebrews 12:28, its only New Testament use). No single English word covers the range. ‘Reverence’ loses the edge the word has before a God who can judge, and ‘fear’ alone can suggest dread without trust. The biblical idea holds both.
ot:
The fear of God appears first as the basic moral restraint a person expects in others. Abraham lies about Sarah in Gerar because he thought, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place” (Genesis 20:11), and the story shows him wrong, since Abimelech, the king of Gerar, behaves with more integrity than he does. After Abraham does not withhold Isaac on Mount Moriah, the angel says, “now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12): fear is shown in what a person will not keep back from God. Jacob names God “the Fear of Isaac” (Genesis 31:42, 53), and Joseph reassures his frightened brothers with “I fear God” (Genesis 42:18), meaning they can expect fair dealing from a man who answers to someone above him. In Egypt the Hebrew midwives “feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed” (Exodus 1:17). The fear of God is what frees them from fear of Pharaoh, and the text twice says God blessed them for it (Exodus 1:20-21).

At the sea, after the rescue from Egypt, “the people feared the LORD and believed in Him” (Exodus 14:31): fear and faith arrive together. At Sinai the thunder and smoke make the people tremble and stand far off, and Moses answers with words that hold the whole doctrine in tension. He tells them, “Do not be afraid,” and then gives the reason: “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning” (Exodus 20:20). There is a fear that drives people away and a fear that keeps them near and obedient, and Moses dismisses the first to plant the second. The law then attaches ‘fear your God’ to commands no human court could enforce: do not curse the deaf or trip the blind (Leviticus 19:14), rise before the aged (Leviticus 19:32), do not take advantage of a neighbor in a sale of land (Leviticus 25:17). God sees what the victim cannot. Deuteronomy teaches that this fear is learned, gathered from hearing God's words (Deuteronomy 4:10) and from the public reading of the law every seven years (Deuteronomy 31:12-13), and it sets fear beside love as one demand: “what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 10:12).

The histories keep fear and exclusive loyalty together. Joshua's call to “fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth” is also a call to “cast aside the gods your fathers served” (Joshua 24:14), and Samuel's farewell says, “Above all, fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart” (1 Samuel 12:24). David's last words picture the just king as one “who rules in the fear of God” (2 Samuel 23:3). Obadiah, a steward in Ahab's court, has “feared the LORD from my youth” (1 Kings 18:12) and quietly hides the LORD's prophets. The settlers placed in Samaria after 722 BC show a counterfeit: in Hebrew they were ‘fearing the LORD’ and serving their own gods (2 Kings 17:33, 41), yet the narrator also says they were not fearing the LORD at all (2 Kings 17:34). A divided fear is no fear. After the exile Nehemiah rebukes nobles who were enslaving their poor neighbors (Nehemiah 5:9) and refuses the governor's customary food allowance “because of my fear of God” (Nehemiah 5:15).

The wisdom books make fear the root of the whole life. Job is introduced as “fearing God and shunning evil” (Job 1:1), and the accuser's question, “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (Job 1:9), is the book's test: is fear of God only a bargain for blessing? The poem on wisdom ends, “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (Job 28:28). Proverbs opens with “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). The word reshit can mean the first step or the chief part, and interpreters differ on which is meant; Proverbs 9:10 uses a different word, techillah, for the starting point, and the book shows fear as both the doorway and the ground of the house. The fear of the LORD is chosen or refused (Proverbs 1:29), found by seeking (2:5), shown in hating evil (8:13), and a source of security and life (14:26-27). It stands against the “fear of man” that “is a snare” (29:25), and the book ends by praising “a woman who fears the LORD” (31:30), so that the fear of the LORD frames the whole collection. Ecclesiastes, after all its searching, concludes, “Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

The Psalms join fear to joy and mercy. “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). God's love and compassion are promised “for those who fear Him” (Psalm 103:11, 13), and the most striking line comes from a penitent: “with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). Forgiveness does not reduce fear; it produces the right kind. Isaiah tells Judah not to fear what the nations fear, because “The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared” (Isaiah 8:13), and he condemns a people whose fear of God is “rules taught by men” (Isaiah 29:13), where the Hebrew noun is yir'ah. The promised king from Jesse's line will have “the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD” and “will delight in the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2-3). Jeremiah hears God promise in the new covenant, “I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me” (Jeremiah 32:40). Jonah traces the whole movement in one chapter: the pagan sailors are afraid of the storm (Jonah 1:5), more afraid when they learn whom Jonah is fleeing (1:10), and finally “feared the LORD greatly” and worshiped him (1:16), while the prophet who says he fears the LORD is running from him. Malachi ends the prophets with a scroll of remembrance “regarding those who feared the LORD” (Malachi 3:16) and the promise that for those who fear God's name “the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2).
nt:
The New Testament does not retire the fear of God; it relocates it around Jesus. Mary's song says that God's “mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation” (Luke 1:50). Jesus tells his disciples not to fear those who can only kill the body and then says, “Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear Him!” (Luke 12:5). In the same breath he adds that not one sparrow is forgotten by God and that “the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid” (Luke 12:7; Matthew 10:28-31). The one to be feared is the Father who counts hairs. The fear of God casts out the fear of people and sits beside trust, not against it. Jesus' parable of the unjust judge describes a man “who neither feared God nor respected men” (Luke 18:2), and the thief on the cross rebukes his companion: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment?” (Luke 23:40).

The Gospels show the fear of the LORD directed at Jesus himself. When Peter sees the miraculous catch he falls at Jesus' knees and says, “Go away from me, Lord,” because “I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8), and Jesus answers, “Do not be afraid” (Luke 5:10). After Jesus stills the storm the disciples were, in Mark's Greek, ‘fearing a great fear’, more afraid in the calm than in the gale, and they ask, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41). Jonah's sailors had feared the LORD with ‘a great fear’ when the sea grew calm, and the echo is hard to miss. At the transfiguration the disciples “fell facedown in terror” until Jesus touched them (Matthew 17:6-7), and the women at the empty tomb fled “trembling and bewildered” (Mark 16:8). The awe once reserved for the LORD at Sinai now meets the person of Jesus. Hebrews adds that Jesus himself lived in godly fear: he prayed “with loud cries and tears,” and “He was heard because of His reverence” (Hebrews 5:7), where the word is eulabeia. The king of Isaiah 11 who delights in the fear of the LORD is the Son who fears his Father perfectly.

In Acts the fear of God marks the church and its edges. After Pentecost “A sense of awe came over everyone” (Acts 2:43), and after the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira “great fear came over the whole church” (Acts 5:11). The church grows “living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 9:31), fear and comfort together. Luke also names Gentiles who attached themselves to the synagogue without becoming Jews: Cornelius is “devout and God-fearing” (Acts 10:2), Peter learns that God “welcomes those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right” (Acts 10:35), and Paul addresses “you Gentiles who fear God” (Acts 13:16, 26). Luke also uses the related term sebomenoi, ‘worshipers’, for such people (Acts 13:43; 16:14). Whether ‘God-fearers’ were a recognized group was debated in the twentieth century, a question taken up below.

Paul's letters hold two sayings together. On one side, “you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship” (Romans 8:15). The fear of the slave who expects the lash is gone. On the other side, Paul tells Gentile believers, “Do not be arrogant, but be afraid” (Romans 11:20), urges the church to perfect holiness “in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1), links his mission to knowing “what it means to fear the Lord” before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10-11), and asks believers to “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21), literally ‘in the fear of Christ’. He tells the Philippians to “work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you” (Philippians 2:12-13); the fear rests on God's work, not on doubt about it. When Paul sums up human sin in Romans 3, his last line is Psalm 36:1: “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Romans 3:18).

The later letters keep the same balance. Hebrews warns, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31), and calls believers who are receiving an unshakable kingdom to worship “with reverence and awe. ‘For our God is a consuming fire’” (Hebrews 12:28-29). Peter writes, “Since you call on a Father who judges each one's work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear” (1 Peter 1:17), and gives a short rule for public life: “fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17), fear being reserved for God. He also rewrites Isaiah 8:12-13: “Do not fear what they fear” is followed by “in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord” (1 Peter 3:14-15), placing Christ where Isaiah placed the LORD of Hosts. John writes, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment” (1 John 4:18). The fear love expels is the dread of punishment, kolasis, not the reverence the rest of the New Testament commends. Revelation's eternal gospel begins, “Fear God and give Him glory” (Revelation 14:7), and heaven's songs ask, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name?” (Revelation 15:4) and summon “those who fear Him, small and great alike” (Revelation 19:5). The fear of God does not end when judgment passes; it becomes the worship of the redeemed.

keyTexts.why: The first time God himself says someone fears him. Abraham's fear is shown in what he would not keep back from God, and it is joined to trust that God will provide.
The midwives fear God and so defy Pharaoh. The fear of God frees them from the fear of the most powerful man in their world, and God blesses them for it.
Moses tells the trembling people not to be afraid, so that the fear of God may keep them from sin. The text distinguishes the fear that flees God from the fear that stays near him.
What God asks is to fear him, walk in his ways, love him, and serve him with the whole heart. Fear and love stand in one sentence as one demand, given for Israel's good.
After a long poem on where wisdom cannot be found, God tells humanity that the fear of the Lord is wisdom and turning from evil is understanding.
If God kept a record of sins no one could stand, but with him is forgiveness so that he may be feared. Mercy produces reverent fear rather than removing it.
The motto of Proverbs: the fear of the LORD is the beginning, or the chief part, of knowledge. All skill in living starts from and rests on a right relation to God.
Do not fear what the crowd fears; the LORD of Hosts alone is to be feared. First Peter applies these words to Christ.
The Spirit of the fear of the LORD rests on the coming king from Jesse's line, and he delights in it. The Messiah is the one who fears God perfectly.
In the everlasting covenant God promises to put his fear in his people's hearts so they will not turn away. Fear becomes a gift of grace, not only a demand.
Jesus commands his friends to fear God rather than those who can only kill the body, and in the same breath tells them the Father numbers their hairs. Fear of God and trust in him belong together.
The growing church walks in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit. Reverence and comfort mark the same community.
Those receiving an unshakable kingdom are to worship with gratitude, reverence, and awe, because God is a consuming fire. The new covenant deepens rather than cancels the awe of Sinai.
Perfect love drives out the fear that has to do with punishment. John distinguishes the slave's dread from the reverence Scripture elsewhere commends.
The eternal gospel proclaimed to every nation opens with the command to fear God and give him glory. The fear of God reaches to the end of the story as worship.

history:
Jewish tradition made the fear of heaven, yir'at shamayim, a central term of piety. The Babylonian Talmud records Rabbi Hanina's teaching that everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven, drawn from Deuteronomy 10:12, meaning that God governs all things but leaves to each person whether to fear him (Berakhot 33b). Maimonides, in the opening book of his law code, the Mishneh Torah (completed about 1180), taught that love and fear of God both arise from contemplating his works: love from glimpsing his infinite wisdom, fear from recognizing how small and limited the one contemplating is (Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah 2:1-2).

Christian reflection has turned largely on how fear relates to love, with 1 John 4:18 and Psalm 19:9 (“The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever”) held side by side. Augustine, in his homilies on 1 John (early fifth century), distinguished servile fear, which dreads punishment, from chaste fear, which dreads losing God and offending him. Love casts out the first; the second endures forever. He compared servile fear to a needle that draws the thread of love into the heart and then passes out of it. The church's liturgy absorbed the fear of the Lord through Isaiah 11:2-3: because the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate render the first mention of fear as ‘piety’ and the second as ‘fear’, Western tradition counted seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, with fear of the Lord among them. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 19, early 1270s) distinguished worldly fear, which turns a person from God to avoid human harm; servile fear, which turns a person to God chiefly for fear of punishment; filial fear, which fears offending God as a child fears grieving a father; and initial fear, a mixture of the last two in those beginning to love. He taught that filial fear, as reverence, remains even in heaven.

The Reformation sharpened the question of fear and assurance. Luther's Small Catechism (1529) explains each of the Ten Commandments with the words ‘We should fear and love God so that...’, joining the two in every line of ordinary obedience. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 12) describes repentance as contrition, the terrors that strike the conscience when sin is recognized, followed by faith that receives forgiveness. Calvin opened his Institutes (1559 edition, 1.2.1) by defining piety as reverence joined with love of God, prompted by knowing his benefits, and he distinguished believers' willing reverence from the forced dread of the ungodly. The Council of Trent (Session 14, 1551) taught that imperfect contrition, or attrition, which may arise from fear of hell and punishment, is not hypocrisy but a gift of God that disposes a sinner toward grace, against Protestant criticism. The Puritan John Bunyan wrote A Treatise of the Fear of God (1679), distinguishing godly fear from the ungodly dread that drives sinners from God. John Wesley's sermon ‘The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption’, on Romans 8:15, described a person awakened by the law who lives in fear as a servant before receiving the Spirit of adoption and living in love as a son.

Modern thought has kept the theme alive in different registers. Søren Kierkegaard took the title of Fear and Trembling (1843) from Philippians 2:12 for his study of Abraham on Mount Moriah. Rudolf Otto's The Idea of the Holy (1917) described the encounter with the divine as mysterium tremendum et fascinans, a mystery that makes a person tremble and yet draws them, which gave scholars of religion a vocabulary for what the Bible calls fear of God. John Murray's Principles of Conduct (1957) closed with an essay on the fear of God, which he treated as the inner life of all godliness and distinguished from the dread of terror. In New Testament scholarship, A. Thomas Kraabel argued in 1981 that the ‘God-fearers’ of Acts were largely Luke's literary creation, but the publication in 1987 by Joyce Reynolds and Robert Tannenbaum of an inscription from Aphrodisias naming many theosebeis, ‘God-worshipers’, alongside Jews persuaded most scholars that such Gentile sympathizers existed, though the date of the inscription and the exact status of the group are still discussed.

differ.view: Roman Catholic and Thomist: servile fear is imperfect but good
differ.body: Following Augustine and Aquinas, this view holds that fear of punishment is a real, if lower, motive that God himself uses. Servile fear can turn a sinner toward God, initial fear mixes it with beginning love, and filial fear, the reverence of a child, matures as love grows and remains forever. The Council of Trent taught that attrition arising from fear of hell, joined to hope of pardon and a will to stop sinning, is a gift of the Holy Spirit and prepares a person for grace in the sacrament of penance. Jesus' command to fear the one who can cast into hell (Luke 12:5) is addressed to his friends, and a sound pastoral theology does not despise the fear that brings people to their knees, while it aims beyond it at love.

differ.view: Lutheran: the terror of the law and the comfort of the gospel
differ.body: Lutheran theology distinguishes law and gospel. The law's threats rightly terrify the conscience, and the Augsburg Confession names these terrors as the first part of repentance. But the terror does not save or earn anything; it drives the sinner to Christ, where the gospel speaks forgiveness and faith receives it. Because the Christian remains both righteous and a sinner in this life, the believer still hears the law's warning as a sinner and the gospel's comfort as one justified. The fear the Small Catechism commends in each commandment is the fear of a child who also loves and trusts, and assurance rests on the promise, not on how much fear or love one feels.

differ.view: Reformed and Puritan: filial fear and the warnings as means
differ.body: Reformed teachers such as Calvin and the Puritans hold that the adopted children of God are freed from slavish dread and live in filial fear, a reverence that grows with assurance rather than competing with it. The sharp warnings of Scripture (Hebrews 10:31; Romans 11:20) are real and addressed to the church, but for the elect they function as means God uses to keep them persevering, not as a suspended threat that true believers may finally fall. Fear of God, on this view, is the soul of godliness, the settled awe that keeps a forgiven person humble, obedient, and near.

differ.view: Wesleyan and Arminian: from the spirit of bondage to the spirit of adoption
differ.body: In Wesley's account an awakened sinner may live for a time under the spirit of bondage, fearing God as a servant, before the Spirit of adoption brings the witness of sonship and love. Because a believer can truly turn away, the warnings of Hebrews and Paul are warnings a real Christian must heed, and a healthy fear of falling is part of watchfulness. Yet the goal is perfect love that casts out tormenting fear (1 John 4:18), and Wesleyans expect that love can so fill a believer in this life that the fear of punishment gives way to the reverent, glad fear of a child.

errors:
The church has rejected two opposite distortions. The first turns the fear of God into servile dread of a capricious power who must be appeased. That was the religion of the nations around Israel, where gods were placated by gifts and even by children, and it returns among Christians as a scrupulous anxiety that never trusts forgiveness. Scripture refuses it: the God to be feared is the one with whom there is forgiveness (Psalm 130:4), who counts the hairs of his children's heads (Luke 12:7), and whose perfect love drives out the fear of punishment (1 John 4:18). A related abuse uses the language of God's fear to control people, so that a leader or parent becomes the one feared. The Bible's fear of God does the reverse. It frees people from fear of Pharaoh, of kings, and of crowds (Exodus 1:17; Isaiah 8:12-13; Proverbs 29:25).

The second distortion shrinks the fear of God into mild respect, a courtesy toward a God who threatens nothing and asks little. This loses the Bible's plain warnings (Hebrews 10:31; 12:29), makes Jesus' command in Luke 12:5 unintelligible, and leaves no ground for the moral seriousness the law attaches to fear, the care for the deaf, the blind, and the debtor where no one else sees. Scripture also exposes a formal fear that goes through religious motions while the heart is elsewhere (Isaiah 29:13) or that fears the LORD while serving other gods (2 Kings 17:33-34). Both are rejected because they are not fear of the living God at all.
life:
The fear of the LORD reorders what a person is afraid of. Someone who fears God takes him more seriously than the opinion of others, the threat of powerful people, or the loss of comfort, and that is why the midwives could defy Pharaoh and why Jesus could tell his friends not to fear those who kill the body. It also shapes ordinary conduct in hidden places: the fair price, the honest word, the care for the weak that no one would notice or punish. The law ties fear to exactly those places.

In prayer, the fear of God keeps intimacy from becoming casual. Christians call God ‘Abba, Father’ by the Spirit and still worship him with reverence and awe, and the two do not cancel each other. Fear rightly held is not the dread of a servant who expects the lash but the care of a child who would not grieve a father, and it sits comfortably with confidence in forgiveness, since God forgives so that he may be feared. For a person troubled by anxious, tormenting fear of God, the New Testament's word is that perfect love drives out the fear of punishment. The awe remains; the terror is answered at the cross.
questions: Moses tells the people at Sinai not to be afraid so that the fear of God may be before them (Exodus 20:20). How would you describe the difference between the two kinds of fear in that verse?

The midwives feared God and not Pharaoh, and Jesus tells his friends to fear God rather than people. Where does the fear of other people most shape your choices, and what would change if the fear of God outweighed it?
Psalm 130:4 says God forgives so that he may be feared, and 1 John 4:18 says perfect love drives out fear. How do these two verses fit together in your understanding of the Christian life?
